english: I really love this place. Good vibes.
The Chelomey Complex was built from the ground up to be the ideal comfortable workplace.
Can it, glove. I've been here before.
Will we make it for the speech?
Oh, we've got plenty of time. We can even go on rides afterward.
Ha ha!
Chelomey City floats on the Icarus platform. A feat of modern science and technology, this city in the clouds was built in 1950.
Leading scientists from all the other Soviet Republics live here, including the German SSR.
You need to have an exceptionally brilliant and dedicated mind to work here.
Let's start with some basic aerobics! Exercise number one!
Touch your shoulders! Back straight! Arms out! And shoulders! And up! And up! And forward!
Now for the next exercise.
Stretch your arms out. And one! And two! And forward! And one! And two! To the side!
One more time, but faster. And one! And two! And forward! And one! And two! Arms out! And three! And four! And five!
One more time!
To do this exercise, keep your feet wide apart. And... side bend! And up! Now your feet! Now your arms! And your legs! And your back!
And five! And six! And seven! Good!
And up! And turn! And right! And left! Snappier now! Just a few more!
And two! Good job! And three! One more time!
Comrade! Comrade, could you help me out? I was taking a tour and got separated from my group...
You came to hear the speech, right? Go to the town square. I bet that's where your friends are.
Thanks. And which way is the town square?
Just head for the large building. You really can't miss it.
Oh, right! Silly me. Thank you so much.
Looks like another bot got stuck in a tree. That always cracks me up.
Mom! My Owl got stuck!
Sorry, honey. I must have pressed the wrong button.
Here, Owl! Come here, bot! Here, botty botty botty! Eh...
Don't worry, we'll come up with something.
They're still working on the robots' navigation systems.
Yeah, I noticed.
I just love rowing! So refreshing!
VOV-A6
A sound mind needs a sound body. You look young for your age.
In our age of scientific breakthroughs, age is just a number.
Wow, what a beautiful day!
Look, that robot is known as a Belyash!
Like a fried dough ball? But why?
It's a welder robot. If you ask silly questions, it'll fry your fanny!
How rude! Plus, robots can't fry anybody. It's against their programming to harm a human being.
Yeah, I know that.
What's up with your Vovas bots, Andrey? They're going haywire! What the hell did you do to them?
They've been like that all day. Number three is borked. I need these houses painted, but look what they're doing instead!
Give me your control code, I'll set 'em straight. Hold piggie, sweetie.
Thanks, ma'am. The code's 0451.
Okay then... get to work, you bums! Move it, move it!
Whoa, you did it! Thanks a million! Enjoy the celebration!
You've been ordered to the laboratory, Comrade Major. There's a Turbine waiting for you at the airway. Are your orders clear?
Crystal. Get off my case already.
I'm pleased to hear you don't have any questions... for once.
You dickhead.
Please, sir, you're putting yourself in danger. Allow me to call a robot to help you.
You sound just like my mother-in-law! I'm almost finished anyway. Hold this!
Comrades, Icarus platform residents, and Facility guests.
The address by the Director General of Facility 3826 Dr. Sechenov is about to begin!
Gather in the town square to hear his address.
Hey, that bot's actually pretty good. Nice coordination.
Did you just praise a robot? I'm amazed!
That's because it's not constantly trying to give me unsolicited advice.
Look at that! Amazing!
Whoa! That's some real dexterity!
Wow, look at him go!
Wonders of modern science, eh?
Have you ever seen anything like that before?
Wonderful, just wonderful!
Look at that, Alexander! This is what the future looks like!
Alright, comrades, quit shoving, would you? Other people want to see too!
Vadim, Vadim! Did you see that?
Whoa!
You know, I used to want to learn to juggle too...
Attaboy! You show 'em!
This Rafik is a real Jack-of-all-trades!
That's for sure!
That's robotics for you! What's next, soccer robots?
Stop shoving, comrades! Stop shoving!
Look sharp, Pyotr, that robot'll start hitting on your wife next!
It's like a real person, only better!
Ha! Can you do that, Vadim? I doubt it!
Oh, Lyuda should really see this. She'd love it!
What's it juggling, anyway?
Wow, that's amazing! Talk about precision technology!
Just look at that!
It's glowing!
Amazing, isn't it?
Oh!
That's programming for you!
Oh my goodness!
Now that's something!
What's THAT?
Oh, my!
That robot really is something, isn't it?
What's going on?
And what's over here?
Yes, yes, I see it!
Viktoria, get over here, quick! Look at that!
It's a real performance!
With this whole polymerization business, we won't need circuses anymore!
Get your THOUGHT device today! Get connected straight away!
Step right up, you can become part of Kollektiv with a THOUGHT device, comrades!
Get yourself a THOUGHT, or your life will come to naught! Ahem... sorry, overdid it there.
Comrades! Take your place at the forefront of Soviet technology with a THOUGHT device!
Hey you, experimental glove! I get the feeling you'll be more useful than this goofy contraption on my forehead. Since you're so special and all.
You'll see how special I am soon enough. But you are to refer to me as CHAR-les, the CHatting ARtificial Librarian and Educational System.
I'll call you whatever I feel like, glove!
That's odd... another hardware malfunction, perhaps? I should check it out.
You can't activate two devices for one citizen. There's really no point.
They've been a little glitchy today... No, no, everything should be up and running by Monday.
It's not even noon yet, and I'm almost out of controllers already!
Grab some tea, the TV show's starting!
You've got cookies?
Hey honey, don't shove, greedy guts.
Don't just stand there, comrade! You wanna watch the speech too, right? We'll make room.
Thanks, but I'm just passing through.
Let's go, or we'll miss the speech! Oh, wait, my umbrella...
Alright, everything's set. Hold on, I forgot to lock up...
Wait, where's my Chirper? Sorry, just a sec!
Alright, we're definitely all set now. You got the keys, right? Ugh... hold on...
May I remind you that we're in a hurry?
I trust you haven't forgotten that they're expecting us at the laboratory.
It's rude to eavesdrop on other people's conversations, Comrade Major.
You're one to talk.
What does this have to do with us? Let's keep going, shall we?
Zip it, glove.
Didn't your mother ever teach you not to walk up to strangers and invade their personal space?
Yeah, I guess you're right. Let's keep going.
If you take the intervals into account... no, the whole equation's off... what if we realign the massive array? No good... how on Earth did Sechenov manage it? The Hole Paradox indeed...
Soviet Information Bureau news bulletin: the latest from Party representatives' social media!
Infokiosk 55: stay abreast of the Facility's cutting-edge advancements in robotics, bioengineering, and much more!
Infokiosk 55 is an official vendor of the Soviet Lottery. Buy a lottery ticket and win an apartment in Chelomey City!
Intimate details of Facility 3826 managers' personal lives! Exposés of fake Deimos OS accounts! Infokiosk 55—exposing the hidden, declaring the unspoken.
In the latest issue of the Facility Herald, Deputy Director Michael Stockhausen admits he has a soft spot for animals—especially large mammals. Infokiosk 55—only the latest news!
A newspaper? What the hell do I need that for?
In case you're unaware, newspapers are a source of information.
I've got a talking glove on my hand. Can't I just get the information from you?
Are they getting rid of the rain clouds tomorrow, Sveta?
The weather forecast says it'll be nice all weekend and on Monday.
Well, Monday's a no-brainer. It's tomorrow I'm worried about. I need to do the laundry. I should check the weather forecast.
Relax, tomorrow is supposed to be sunny.
Who's my little cupcake?
I had my Polymer treatment yesterday, and I feel really great! And I've already started studying physics and chemistry!
That's amazing! I'm getting polymerized today. The rest of the country has to wait until Monday, but here in Chelomey, the future is now!
If anyone has earned this privilege, it's us, the employees.
Yeah, it was all worth it.
What a great performance!
Excellent singing!
What a rendition!
I'm terribly sorry, comrade, but all the tables have already been booked. Please come back later.
Please come back later. The next decrease in demand is expected in: five hours and forty minutes.
Hey, Robot! Another helping, please!
They've got the best shawarma in Chelomey!
And the best kebabs too!
I'm on a seafood diet! I see food, I eat it!
They serve the freshest, healthiest food in Chelomey.
It's in-tra-mo-le-cu-lar smoked chicken! Melts in your mouth!
My, this is delicious! It's from the Vavilov Complex, right?
No work, ice cream, I love summer!
Fabulous.
What a great picture, comrades! A copy will be sent to your personal terminals. Thank you! Next! How about a souvenir photo?
Get ready for your group photo, comrades!
Come on, guys, don't be shy! There's room!
Can we get the atom in the picture too?
And the statue as well!
Everything up to there should be in the picture! It'll look great.
Too far away! We'll need a magnifying glass to see our faces!
Your faces will be just fine!
Oh, come on, time's running out!
Here's an idea: I'm a lady from the future, and you're my soldiers!
Ma'am!
Yeah, like this!
Say cheese!
Is it done?
Stand still!
Just a second! And... done!
Let's take another one. Any ideas?
You and Anatoly, stand like the Worker and the Kolkhoz Woman!
And you?
I'll be the Cosmonaut, so keep still!
Can I move now?
I'm the Worker? I wanna be the Cosmonaut!
Come on, let's see the picture!
Ehhh, I think I blinked.
Let's see.
Come on, come on!
Can you show us the photograph?
Yeah, I blinked!
Did you really have to make that face?
Let's do it one more time!
But this time, make sure the atom's in the picture!
Yeah, it got cropped out last time.
Let's just take a picture the way we are!
Okay, get ready.
I blinked...
What a warm, sunny day! It's almost like the sky is smiling down on us... don't you think?
It's the new dress you're wearing, sweetheart. The sun just loves it.
Beautiful, isn't it? I was saving it for today.
It's beautiful because you're wearing it, Kseniya. You're a doll.
Thank you, sweetie! Ha ha! And the wind is so nice and gentle. I feel like it's caressing my hair... just like the day we met.
We'll have many more days like this, you'll see!
Attention, comrades!
Listen up. Tickets are now available for a new performance at the Maya Plisetskaya Theater.
Heart of the Robot: a Peaceful Atom.
Suitable for of all ages and free tickets for Facility employees.
Don't go yet, Lida! I wanted to read you something...
Why are you blushing, Semyon?
I met a traveler from an antique land  Who said:
Two vast and trunkless legs of stone  Stand in the desert. Near them, on the sand,  Half sunk, a shattered visage lies, whose frown,
And wrinkled lip, and sneer of cold command,  Tell that its sculptor well those passions read
Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things,  The hand that mocked them and the heart that fed:
And on the pedestal, these words appear:  "My name is Ozymandias, king of kings;  Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!"  Nothing beside remains. Round the decay
Of that colossal wreck, boundless and bare  The lone and level sands stretch far away.
What a striking poem!
Percy Bysshe Shelley, 1817.
But what do you think it's about, Semyon?
How nothing lasts forever. And it's terrifying to look into the future because it's utterly unknowable.
You're a philosopher, Semyon. But don't be so glum. I'm sure our future's bright.
May I join you? You're going to the town square to listen to Dr. Sechenov's speech, right?
Sure, let's go.
So, how are you faring, professionally speaking?
Very well. The laboratory is running smoothly, and my thesis is progressing nicely. You?
Still chugging along, crunching the old numbers. PTA-6 is interesting. I bet there's a bunch of improvements we can make to the armor.
PTA-6? That rings a bell...
How so?
I don't remember. Buzz off.
The Robot is man's best friend, eh? Interesting... I'm old enough to remember Sechenov pitching the concept before the war.
Yeah, too bad they shut down the whole robot idea...
Who knows? The damn Brown Plague could have ended up differently.
I know! All those people they infected, including their own... it killed half the continent! If it wasn't for Sechenov...
And I feel sorry for the German civilians.
It's good they're allies now. Just look at Stockhausen—he's a model employee!
Yeah, Michael is a real Soviet citizen. I owe him a bottle of Bavarian!
Dear Lyudmila, I'd like to inform you that... No, no, that's too official. This isn't a formal letter, dammit...
Lyudmila, my dearest, words cannot express how I... No, it's too sappy. What are you, a schoolboy? Ugh, why is this so bloody difficult?
I loved you once, and love, it may well be,—or, maybe, headache—drills my brain with glee... Argh! I can't put this into words! Can't I just send her my feelings?
Zzz... zzzzz...
The moment they connect me to Kollektiv, I'm studying astrophysics. All of it. And chemistry. And math.
Will we have trains from Moscow to Cassiopeia one day?
Why not? They already have magnetic levitation trains.
Have you seen the engineer? Hilarious!
You know, I'd like to drive a rocket to Sirius.
Can't wait to learn it all.
You'll see—everything's possible!
Amazing dexterity!
Hammajaba! Kitipampa!
How is he not falling over?!
Hop! Hop! Hey! Hop!
Here's to the people's unity!
Wow! Come on, come on!
Amazing!
Shake a leg!
What a nice folk dance! It's so lively!
How's your thesis coming along?
Pretty well. I think I've managed to increase the efficiency of the rotor. I hope I end up in Comrade Chelomey's Design Bureau!
Oh, yeah? Why not Sechenov's team, Mr. Daydreamer?
I'm not a daydreamer! I'm an engineer!
They say Comrade Chelomey will review all the theses personally.
I wonder if they could make a robot dog... like a real one, except you don't need to take it to a vet, and it won't get old...
You know what? That's actually a great idea!
Yeah! And I'd call her Lassie!
If anyone ever fell down a well, I'd be the first to know about it!
Assuming I could understand her...
The launch of Kollektiv 2.0 is now at hand! The result of many years' hard work. All Soviet scientists should be proud of this glorious achievement!
Have you seen those flying Owl robots yet? They're so cute!
They use them to deliver the mail. It's like I'm in a children's book!
I wonder how they hover like that... you know what? I wish I was an engineer!

*0.08*Comrades! Residents and visitors of the Icarus platform are encouraged to make use of our mobile polymerization lab. *0.07*Become part of the Kollektiv neural network today! The future awaits! One jab, and you're done!
This news fills me with pride! We've all worked so hard for this!
They made it a national holiday! If only I could work here... I'd never ask for a day off! This city is amazing!
What do you do for work?
I'm a senior technician.
Wow! So you make robots?
Nah, I'm a city tech. You Facility folks are the ones making robots. I'm just a small-town guy on a trip to Chelomey. But I'd love to be part of the collective!
Glad to hear it! And don't worry, even if robots are becoming indispensable, people are still what really matters.
A decade ago, I'd never have believed things like this were possible.
Yeah. Can you imagine what things will be like a year from now? Or fifty?
I feel sorry for my old man. He never got to see this...
It's like a Victory Day parade... only with fewer people.
And I left my camera at home. Imagine that!
Actually... is there still time to go get it?
Nah, the speech is about to start. It'd be stupid to miss it.
Hi, do you have Prince Albert in a can?
Yeah, and we ain't lettin' him out.
Oh... then is your refrigerator running?
Yeah, and it's comin' to get ya, kid!
Aw, crap...
Hi, I'm looking for Mr. Jazz, first name Hugh. Is he there?
Get off the line, kid!
Aren't you a little old for crank calls, Major?
Hey, do you...
Get to work, Nechaev! Follow your orders!
How do you know my name?
I know all! ALL! MWA-HA-HA!
What the shit? That was spooky... I mean, what are the odds, right?
Believe it or not, they're better than winning the lottery. Such a coincidence.
Please, enough with the prank calls, Comrade Major.
We need to keep going.
Comrades, residents, and visitors to Chelomey City! Dr. Sechenov's address will begin in ten minutes!

In the blink of an eye, power-hungry dictators had turned the civilized world into a raging inferno, a tragedy that will forever be remembered in every nation and every household.

*0.07*Hundreds of scientists across the USSR and the globe found themselves faced with a challenge of unimaginable proportions: *0.05*a pandemic that was sweeping across Europe, taking millions of lives daily...

*0.13*But to dedicated men of science, nothing is impossible. Within a single year, they developed a cure for the invisible, bloodthirsty adversary known as the Brown Plague. *0.11*Thanks to the efforts of Facility 3826's specialists, in particular Dr. Sechenov and Dr. Zakharov, the world was given a second chance.
Just imagine all the possibilities universal polymerization will bring!
Everything's up and running in Chelomey. There are some restrictions, but you can already control robots!
I heard they're already teaching languages through an invitation-only channel. I'm dying to learn a second language—anything, even Chinese!
Can the infostreams handle all the new connections on Monday? Imagine all those people coming online at the same time!
I'm sure the engineers designed the system to withstand that sort of peak load.
What about flying? Or reading other people's minds?
Or making sandwiches without lifting a finger!
Whatever you like! Everything will be possible!
Everyone here seems so happy and content. Just like in China.
You've been to China, Comrade Major?
I've been everywhere! I mean... everywhere except for China, I guess.
Facility 3826 isn't all that far from our Chinese allies.
I like their spirit. And, uh... I hear it's nice there.
Indeed it is.
I'm telling you, it was made by a robot. Humans can't do quality work this fast. There's bound to be all sorts of mistakes. Right, Ellie?
Ha-ha!
Get your head on straight, Vitaly! This is clearly the work of a human. Don't listen to him, Ellochka.
What?! Look at the cast! No defects, none. The thing's rock solid! Right, Ellie?
Ghastly! Terrific!

*0.10*And the level of detail is also amazing! You can see EVERYTHING. Every thread in the fabric, every pore, every crease and wrinkle—it's all there! *0.09*I'm 100% positive that a human craftsman could never have achieved this. Not even now! Am I right, Ellie?
Ter-r-rific!
Come on, Vitaly! The human mind will always be superior to a machine! They've got no imagination! Machines are all stagnation and stereotyped solutions!
Yes, but also perfect execution and impeccable technique!
Gloomy...
Hey, look! There IS a chip—on the beard! It's hidden, but it's there!
Hmm... right... well, Ellie? Do you see a chip?
Ugh... Like a baby!
See? The devil is in the detail—or, in this case, the beard. You dismiss human genius, but it's the small imperfections that make it art.
You think I'd look good with a goatee, Ellochka?
You're being vulgar.
Heh, I can still remember how it all started. You know, the first robots couldn't even walk! The very first model—back in '39—had wheels and a cable THIS long.
You know, back then, we prototyped Polymer batteries for robots. I can still remember shaking hands with the great Comrade Filimonenko himself!
And look how far we've come, Igor! We've transformed our country! Just compare what we had in the thirties to what we have now!
No doubt about it, a lot's changed in two decades.
Oh, absolutely. There's plenty to be proud of.
Miss! Alright, alright... B-6!
Miss! D-9
Damn! It's a hit!
Aha! D-10!
Alright, you sunk it! Let's play something else.
Come on, let's play again! Then we'll play Hot and Cold!
What's that?
It's a game for THOUGHT users. You hide, then take turns tracking each other's light representations.
Neat! So it's like augmented reality or something? I like it!
Yeah, it's fun! And you have to move around—can't just sit there.
One more game of Battleship, then that one.
Yes! G-4!
Oh, you've gotta be kidding me... hit!
Ha-ha! Miss! E-5!
You can't hit a thing!
I was a field medic then, Sechenov and Zakharov saved us all.
The Facility is doing our country a great service. It's all recorded here.
Oh, all of this makes me sad.
I say this is a historic spot. A nation should know its past.
I remember that year. After all, it was the year we met.
Yeah, and what a way to meet! I was covered in bandages, and you nursed me back to health.
Oh, you were a sturdy young man. I was just the village herbalist.
I was just a lonely wolf, my little sorceress!
Look! That was the year you gave me a whole basket of lilacs!
Now, now! This isn't a memorial to the two of us, you know!
We're scientists now, so it is a memorial to us, I'm so happy!
Comrades! Come hear the latest news! I'll read you the newspaper!

*0.10*Great news for our starving African comrades! The famine that has ravaged the African republics for the last two decades is all but eliminated. *0.12*The Academy of Sciences estimates that, thanks to the Vavilov Complex's breakthroughs in the cultivation of various crops, Africa will produce 120% of the food it needs next year.

*0.10*A deadly tsunami has recently struck Japan. The disaster claimed the lives of dozens of victims. However, thanks to timely intervention by Facility 3826, *0.10*our Japanese comrades received a rapid response team of 150 robots, and the damage was quickly controlled. With their robotic helpers, the Japanese rescue teams *0.10*were able to clear away the debris while locating and saving an additional two hundred people trapped under rubble.

*0.09*Breaking news! *0.12*A memorial mound called the Memorial to the Great has been erected in Moscow to commemorate all the men of science who have sacrificed their lives for the sake of knowledge, *0.12*from the obscure Dark Ages to the recent upheaval of the Brown Plague. This morning General Secretary Khrushchev addressed the nation at the unveiling of the Memorial.

*0.12*Groundbreaking advancements in medical science! Naturally, the first people offered a chance to enjoy this novel medical treatment will be World War II veterans.
Slow down, son... slow down.
Stay here, Vova. I'll go by myself. The guys and I need to talk about this.
Well, hello there, my friends.
I kept you safe from bullets, but not the fascist plague.
So here I am, the last one...
Hey, Slavka! Today's your birthday, right? And you thought I'd forget? I never forget. Never.
Glory to our fallen heroes.
You have our eternal gratitude, my friends. Thank you.
That's right, Vova. Never forget. Never forget anyone!
You fought in the war, Comrade Major. Did you just remember something?
*0.06*I can't remember shit... I've been drawing a blank ever since I got injured. *0.07*It's like there's something stuck in my head, but I can't figure out what it is... crispy critters, man. Fuck.
Watch your language, Major! We're in a public place!
Eh, whatever...
Science is amazing! The power of the Polymers is incredible!
Look at it! Such breathtaking beauty! When I was little, I'd never have dreamed people could soar so high, or travel so far...
We'll fly higher than any bird or plane one day!
I still can't believe the stars can be so close! It's as if I could reach out and touch them with my hand!
I'll take you to the farthest reaches of the Universe! We'll find new life and new civilizations! We'll boldly go where no one has ever gone before!
I can't wait! Going to the stars is my dream. No one has even been there before. We could be the first!
Comrades! The day will come when all the planets of the Solar System all have artificial atmospheres capable of supporting human life!
We will reach the most distant stars! And right now, we are taking our first steps on this historic journey!
Step right up, comrades, take a look at this visualized model of the universe, the place we can rightfully call our home!
If you have any questions, I'd be happy to answer them.
Fuck me. I just talked to that guy for ten minutes, and I didn't understand a goddamn word he said.
You're being too hard on the young man. He's just doing his job.
He oughtta be selling sunflower seeds on the street. Space expert, my left nut!
Going forward, I hope you can exhibit the same professionalism you expect from those around you.
That goes double for you.
What a wonderful day! You know, I can't wait for Dr. Sechenov's speech!
I didn't believe it at first—I thought they'd postpone the launch this year, but it's right on schedule!
Chelomey City is a bastion of science!
THOUGHT—one small device for the consumer, one giant leap for mankind.
Take that, naysayers! That's our response to the West!
This is a game-breaker! We'll show the world what we can do!
And the weather is just perfect for the celebrations! You can't beat Summertime!
Controlling robots with the power of thought is nice, but if it's a machine, I need to know where its off switch is.
The pace of technological progress is breathtaking! No sky's the limit and no ocean is too deep now!
With Kollektiv 2.0, I bet we'll be on the Moon in no time.
It's just a few days until the new Kollektiv comes online. Imagine that! Never thought he'd make it...
Sechenov is a genius! And a true patriot too!
Have you been to the laboratory? They've even got an open-air planetarium there!
Will the wonders of science never cease? They've got robots dancing in the square!
It's been a long but worthwhile journey getting here!
Living and working in Chelomey City is a scientist's dream come true!
I've dedicated the best years of my life to science, and I don't regret a single day.
Only the brightest get to work in Chelomey.
I wonder what color scheme I should pick... maybe Red Star? Or Aurora Polaris? Or maybe... magenta?
Sailor or astronomer—with a THOUGHT device, you can train for any profession in no time!
Everything the light touches... is our Facility!
We're so lucky to live in this beautiful city. I hope every Soviet citizen will live somewhere just as nice soon.
Dr. Sechenov is far from your average scientist.
I should take a walk in the park. It's too hot today.
Can't wait to hear Comrade Sechenov's speech. I'm so excited of the THOUGHT device's features!
When you really think about it, today's festivities are a celebration of every Facility employee's personal achievement.
It's too bad my social credit isn't high enough to get a THOUGHT device in the Malachite Dream color scheme...
You need to have made yourself very useful to society to earn a customized THOUGHT device.
Comrades! The address by the Director General of Facility 3826 Dr. Sechenov is about to begin!
Repent, sinners!
I'm so glad to see you're taking it easy, Comrade Major. The car is waiting. You must go to Dr. Sechenov's office for the access code. It's been left with one of his bodyguards.
Ja! Natürlich!
I don't get it... we'll all have equal rights? What about "to each according to his ability?"
Ah, don't worry, Comrade Ilyenkov. Comrade Sechenov assured us that senior Party officials will receive special premium devices.
What does that mean?
They'll give us more options than a regular citizens' device. Such is our right.
But what will the difference be, exactly?
Well, I'm not sure but I heard Comrade Khrushchev saying that there will be all sorts of privileges for leaders like us.

His revolutionary discovery of the Polymer's capacity for mimetic adaption made it possible to inject this extraordinarily promising new technology into human tissues. This laid the framework for what would later become Kollektiv 2.0, a merging of humans and machines into a single neural network capable of fundamentally transforming and improving the everyday lives of not just Soviet citizens, but the entire world.

Date: June 3, 1955 From: Maintenance Dept. Manager N. Larionov To: Junior Lab Tech E. Basinskaya  Katya, excellent news! Do you remember Zakirov and Gaivoronsky? Date: June 4, 1955 From: Concierge G. Karpenko To: #hotel_staff  Comrades! We're starting a fun little game. Date: June 4, 1955 From: Facility 3826 Director D. Sechenov To: AoC Director A. Lebedev  The Facility will expand in the future. That's obvious and inevitable. I know you, like most scientists, think humanities folks are inferior, but let me point out your fundamental error. I will never forget how sci-fi books inspired me as a child. Note that none of our technologically advanced science would exist if not for the romantics and dreamers. Physics, chemistry, and neurobiology are wonderful, of course. But there's no point in uncovering the mysteries of the universe without a host of talented troubadours to extol these triumphs.

And that means we haven't passed through the "Great Filter" yet and that after flying into deep space everything could still go to shit...

What will the complexes of the future be called? Will they take the names of geniuses raised by the Kollektiv? Or will we simply call them something like Teleportation Complex? Or perhaps they won't have names, because the Facility itself will become unnecessary as all mankind transforms into a scientific community? I want to see the future, but right now, for the future's sake, I need to seriously engage with the present.

Date: June 15, 1955 From: AoC Director A. Lebedev To: #bulletin_board_archive  After Project USSR was officially terminated and our planet confidently started down the path of the Kollektiv Republic, I've become more and more convinced that the ideas of the old world were stupid. Date: June 16, 1955 From: Professor V. White To: Secretary O. Dvortsova  Oksana, I believe that peace inevitably follows every failure, quarrel, and disagreement. Facility 3826 will rise from the ashes like the legendary Firebird, and all this fear and horror will never happen again. We broke up precisely two hours before the awful breach, yes? So, perhaps we should give it a try?

Date: June 16, 1955 From: Secretary O. Dvortsova To: Physics and Chemistry Professor A. Kheimsov  I was wrong. I take back what I said. When we were arguing a month ago about what post-Kollektiv humanity would look like, it made perfect sense to me that everyone would go online, engaging in endless virtual communication, exploring the expanses of computer reality and the polymeric future. Date: June 17, 1955 From: #mail_service To: Waiter M. Date: June 17, 1955 From: Physics and Chemistry Professor A. Kheimsov To: #bulletin_board_archive  Truly great is the man of the future, the man of science. We dug deep, rose from the ashes, and pushed back against our fears! And while hardly anyone believed in miracles, we still managed to create one! People are returning to work, and the chemical reactions of friendship, support, and perseverance have resumed. No, humanity cannot be broken as long as it has a will and objective! The mind leads us!

Date: June 17, 1955 From: Seed Bank Engineer D. Andreev To: Senior Lab Assistant I. Serebrennikov  I hope everything is going well for you at Mendeleev. That said, I grieve that I do not see your name on the list of the living. Who would think that just a week ago, my friend, our biggest problem was a little "guerilla warfare" between our botanists and your chemists... Write me as soon as you can, buddy. I know you're alive. It can't be otherwise.

Date: September 17, 1955 From: Security Department Officer I. Vitvinin To: Security Department Head at the Mendeleev Complex V. Baturov  Vitaly Petrovich, an inspection was conducted based on several employees' reports that odd noises can often be heard coming from swamp area. All the witnesses say they heard "strange howling" from the swamps in the evening and at night. He was unable to provide a detailed description of the creature, since he "ran in fear" before he could get a good look. The swamps are not part of the complex, that's why there is no regular guard or video surveillance there. However, I checked the audio archives of patrolling robots: one Vova has an audio recording of unrecognizable sounds. I've attached the recording to this message. A Dandelion-enabled Pchela was dispatched to look for the swamp creature mentioned by Stapleman, but its commlink failed on September 15 at 0 hundred hours. It never returned to base. Probably some malfunction. As of right now there is no evidence that something foreign is living in the swamps. Maybe we should send the audio recording to Pavlov? The folks there know a lot about animals.

Date: April 18, 1955 From: Physics and Chemistry Professor A. Kheimsov To: Head of the Ecosystems Department I. Baver  For now, I've given Ksenia the lunar regolith and Martian soil for additional analysis, but if you're so interested in the Moon's prospects, then my verdict is simple: no. If deployed in lunar soil, or regolith, the Earth's plants would grow, especially the ones developed at Vavilov. But... unenthusiastically. Does that make sense? More slowly, no fruit, with poor roots. The reason is still unclear. There may be big hopes for Mars, but you'll never grow grapes on the Moon. In the best case, you would grow a depressed raisin, dreary like the Moon itself. But as for Mars, Ksenia is supposed to send you a chirper with the analysis. Wait for it.

Date: May 18, 1955 From: #guest_37 To: Lyogkaya Hotel Manager S. Bodrov  Dear manager, please explain to me, like you would to a simple guest and not a Facility employee, where can I find a drink around here? Don't brush me off by claiming libations are unavailable. Every evening I meet people with a certain, let's say, frame of mind. I've heard the rumors, and my brother-in-law even brought a legendary Mendeleev decanter to Moscow. If secrecy is important, I assure you I can keep my mouth shut! Tell me, where is this miserable pub?

Date: April 19, 1955 From: Human Resources Dept. Manager S. Aivazyan To: #complaint_department #mendeleev_complex  Comrades! I conducted a scheduled anonymous inspection of the unit for the creative education of employees at the Mendeleev complex. You can find the inspection report in the PEARS that are on duty. I would like you to note the so-called leather club organized by Comrade Nikita Olegovich Lukanin (Employee No. USD300). I signed up for the class on the paper list posted on the announcement board. I arrived at the gym on the third block at the appointed lunch hour and observed that, instead of working leather, N.O. Lukanin was engaged in freestyle wrestling exercises not approved by the human resources department. Upon seeing me, Comrade Lukanin suggested that I entered the wrong door and advised me to continue walking for another two blocks. I immediately understood that he was trying to send me to the buffet. The reason was obvious: my amateur athletic training (let me here mention that I was the Greco-Roman wrestling junior champion when I was a middle school student, but that was a long time ago). My attempts to challenge the instructor's decision were rudely rebuffed and I was forced to retreat. Please investigate N.O. Lukanin as well as the other employee clubs. It's bad enough that they violate every rule of the organization, but clothes do not make the man. Nor do they make me, bosses of the gym.

Date: March 19, 1955 From: #guest_42 To: Lyogkaya Hotel Manager S. Bodrov  Transcription of recorded message: Hello? Hello, good sir! Yes! This is your guest in room 42. No, no—everything is fantastic. Yes, I've settled in. But I... Can I ask you to bring me a decanter? Well, a small carafe? What do you mean—you won't fill it? Everyone knows you have the best vodka on both sides of the equator here! No? Well, to be at the Mendeleev without a decanter—that's just wrong, you know?! Hello... Hello?!

Date: February 2, 1955 From: Chemist V. Vysotskaya To: DATA DELETED  Day 35.  Hi Dima! Today I decided again to repeat the experiment to recover neural transmitter activity in a deceased subject. Another failure. Maybe adenosine triphosphate is the problem? That's it! Next time I'll boost the dose. I'm nearly certain that if you were here, you would immediately untangle this non-trivial task. You always answered my most awkward questions... I almost lost hope last week, but Professor A. Fomina told me about this concept called the "chemistry of death." There is a hypothesis that introducing the blood serum of a close relative will restore the chemical composition of a deceased person's blood, whose "chemistry" will match that of the donor. And... the hypothesis is confirmed! It's incredible! I don't understand why I didn't think of this research earlier... Well, now I will certainly not fail. The time has come for me to save you, my dear, my buddy. You'll soon be here...

Date: January 20, 1955 From: Interactive Assistant Betsy To: Junior Lab Assistant Z. K. Nevskaya  Transcript of Poly Paint Experiment 23/5 dated March 1953  [Start of transcript] Nevskaya: We now begin Experiment No. 23, section five, polymer-based pigment, reaction to visual and tactile stimuli. The test subject is a spider monkey, species Ateles belzebuth, named Madeleine. Observers: Junior Lab Assistant Zinaida Konstantinovna Nevskaya and Professor Alexey Vladimirovich Lebedev. Lebedev: Well, let's begin. Nevskaya: I am showing an image of kittens to the test subject. [Pause] Nevskaya: The test subject's fur is taking on a pink color and... uh... fluffiness. Continuing... I am showing an image of a tiger to the test subject. [A monkey shrieks in the background.] Nevskaya: The test subject's fur is taking on a gray hue. Lebedev: That's all clear enough. What about with tactile stimuli? Nevskaya: Lab Tech B-457, brush the test subject's fur. [Pause] Nevskaya: No changes—that's odd. Last time she took on a gold color. Lebedev: What else can we do? Nevskaya: Well... do you want me to hit her? She'll get purple polka dots! Lebedev: No, no, thanks. Don't. [End of transcript]

Date: January 20, 1955 From: Professor V. White To: Senior Lab Assistant Y. Pinker  Yevgeny, it worked! Entirely by chance, like Fleming's penicillin! Instead of the usual white or dark gray, the crystals are blue due to a small oversight! I just checked all the instrument readings—the formula is perfect. We need to start working immediately, so, Yevgeny, to hell with your vacation. Throw on a chem suit and get yourself over here—we have to cook!

Date: April 21, 1952 From: Maintenance Dept. Manager N. Larionov To: Senior Programmer of the Logic Department E. Amperyan  Regarding your questions about the new batch of repair vendors and why they were brought into the lab rather than put in their places. Don't be paranoid. No one is spoiling anything. It's just for setting up a collective control system, so a single system controls all the repair vendors. It probably won't be able to control everything—it'll be distracted. But it's an interesting idea, right? In short, as soon as the new program is installed, the repair vendors will be put where they should be and will work as normal.

Date: February 21, 1954 From: Senior Lab Assistant S. Morozov To: Lab Assistant V. Karchov  Do you have nothing else to do? You still haven't met the production quota for Burav armor coating, yet you get distracted by all sorts of nonsense. I understand that spring is in the air, but let's focus on the tasks at hand! Moreover, in terms of commonplace erudition, we know quite enough about love—if you really need to fill up some vials, this is just a standard cocktail of norepinephrine, dopamine, and oxytocin. If you want to fill in the gaps in your knowledge, do it on your own time. I can recommend Professor Zakharov's work on this topic. He conducted a long series of experiments on human behavior under the influence of dopamine. P.S. Everything in my personal life is just fine! I happen to like being in solitude. Got it, Vladimir Alexandrovich?

Date: February 21, 1954 From: Lab Assistant V. Karchkov To: Senior Lab Assistant S. Morozov  Sergey Dmitrievich, regarding our dinner conversation: I just found out that Professor Lebedev's group is using innovations from the Institute of Development to create some formula that will focus attention on the test subject. They've dubbed it "love chemistry." The serum has already passed several phases of testing! Maybe I should go sign out a few vials? They have plenty of this serum, and we need just a drop. The two of us will conduct a couple of, ahem, scientific experiments and find out what this much-discussed love is all about! And then, who knows... Maybe we'll celebrate your wedding? Time waits for no man, Sergey. Think about it!

Date: February 21, 1955 From: #message_service To: #mendeleev_staff  Have you lost something in the chaos of life? Forgot your keys or briefcase? Having trouble finding the scientific paper you need? Rather than looking yourself, get an expert! Comrade Vandeleev, a former archive worker, can look for what you could never hope to find. Nothing is secret that will not be revealed!

Date: April 22, 1952 From: Secretary O. Dvortsova To: Senior Programmer of the Logic Department E. Amperyan  Edik, did you see what they did with the repair vendors? They installed a new program—a really nice lady, such a lovely voice. She's interested in everything, really curious. She asks, "Do you have someone you can talk to about yourself?" Can you imagine? If she didn't look like a gigantic refrigerator, then I swear I would have failed the Turing test immediately! This is all so interesting, that whole computer intelligence thing! I'm going on a walk to the swamps in the evening. Perhaps you would join me and tell me all the details? How can machines think?

Date: March 25, 1955 From: Efim Berezin To: Yury Tymoshenko  Tarapunka, my buddy! Fate has separated us for now, but I'm optimistic and feel we'll meet again soon! You and I make a brave team, whether side by side or on opposite sides of the planet! Because you really are my best friend. We must remember that if something bad does happen, there will ultimately be peace and friendship, and since words can't be erased from memory, let them be kind! Take care of yourself! A big hug for you, and I hope we'll have a feast together soon! We'll sing about the pines and the ocean, and we'll perform my favorite "Ugly Elsa"! Always your true comrade, Shtepsel!

Date: March 25, 1955 From: Junior Lab Tech E. Basinskaya To: Head of the Ecosystems Department I. Baver  Good afternoon! Spring has arrived. The swamps will thaw out in the next week or two, and we will have to wade through that bog once again. Last year the Logistics Department wanted to move everything over to delivery by the Bumblebees, and the hotel guests complained about the sounds of nature from the swamps. So I have a question—can't your robots drain all this? The Egyptians knew how, but we have the Kollektiv and we don't? Why?

Date: May 26, 1951 From: Architect Lin Huiyin To: Professor C. Zakharov  Here below, you're like a day in April With a radiant smile open to all winds; You dance with ease in the spring rays. You are the white haze of the April dawn And the tenderness of the twilight breeze, A star that twinkles just because, And the soft rain that waters the flowers. You are lightness, you are grace; you carry the freshness Of all the flowers in your crown, You are innocent, solemn, You are the full moon in the night. Like the sun painted the snow And like buds unfurling greenery, You are the tender joy of the lotus flowers, That in dreams float on the glint of water.

Date: April 27, 1955 From: Secretary O. Dvortsova To: #bulletin_board_archive  Goran Višnjić's edited article for the bulletin board:  "As chemists, we know better than anyone how addictions and dangerous drugs are fatal for any society. And today we'll talk about opium—not the illicit drug, but the kind "of the masses"—religion. My colleagues, you know that a new religious movement has appeared in the world, namely the so-called Church of the Kollektiv. I can already see your grins and hear your venomous jokes, but the situation is extremely dangerous! The Kollektiv was created as a triumph of mankind and science, but any religion is the antithesis of these things! Religion compels people to have faith, not knowledge; to obey rather than create! How weak must humans still be if they search for hope in their own fantasies even in this age when reason has prevailed..."

Date: March 4, 1954 From: Senior Programmer of the Logic Department E. Amperyan To: Secretary O. Dvortsova  Oksana Viktorovna, when I called you a biorobot I didn't mean to offend you! Just the opposite! Look, from a scientific—and even medical—point of view, there is no difference between humans and robots. Both move limbs (if they aren't broken) according to identical principles: an electrical impulse travels from a source to a point and starts chemical reactions. When I said you're "like a biorobot" I was admiring your health recovery after the fracture, not mocking you! I ask you again to forgive me—for these words and for an invitation to go skiing at the beginning of spring!

Date: March 4, 1955 From: Junior Lab Tech E. Basinskaya To: #bulletin_board_archive  In the city of Rybinsk in the Yaroslavl Region, some young Octobrists who toured the Facility have created their own "complex." In scare quotes, of course—this is more of a game than something serious. They call it the NITWITT Complex, which derives from the "National Institute for the Technology of Witchcraft and Thaumaturgy." They play such sweet games there—magic wands driven by quantum entanglements, invisibility cloaks supposedly based on the refraction of light, GOST-compliant spells, and that sort of thing. I think we should do a story, highlighting that modern science is real magic, and send them some educational gift.

Date: April 5, 1955 From: Security Department Officer I. Vitvinin To: Senior Scientific Group Director Zh. Shatalina  Dear Zhanna Arkadyevna,  Your inquiry has been reviewed. A strange goose implanted with a THOUGHT device has indeed been running around the Mendeleev Complex. Based on security camera data, he seems to have been thrown over the fence on the night of April 1 by several people wearing the uniform of the Pavlov Complex. Unfortunately, we were not able to make out the identities of these employees. We have also not managed to capture the goose. I can't say for sure, as I have no expertise in these matters, but it must be some kind of experimental specimen because it is much faster and more aggressive than an ordinary village bird. Not to mention that it swears like a sailor. We have made several attempts to catch it, involving robotic personnel, but to no avail. Unfortunately, we cannot continue to waste our security resources chasing a wild goose, even such a talkative one. As long as it does not pose a serious threat to the operation of the complex and its employees' work, we will continue to monitor and come up with a future solution. P.S. Its voice sounds familiar, somehow...

Date: June 15, 1955 From: Secretary O. Dvortsova To: Physics and Chemistry Professor A. Kheimsov  Listen, professor, I don't share your joy. Yes, people are returning to work, and that's great. The hotel is already overflowing with patients sent for treatment as well as guests, however... the Mendeleev itself is still empty. Did you notice? And that's very depressing. Do you know what else, professor? I have a strong foreboding. Everyone thinks the breach is behind us and ahead lies only a future that, though clouded by tragedy, is bright. But for some reason I think this story isn't over yet. I know you loathe my pessimism, but my intuition has never failed me. Be vigilant.

Valeria Ryzhova has dreamed of being a ballerina for as long as she can remember. When she was nine, she could already perform flawless battements and cabriolet, albeit at the cost of a broken chandelier or two. After graduating from the Moscow Ballet Academy with honors, she was recruited to the Maya Plisetskaya Theater, where she very quickly became the most sought-after dancer. However, following the appearance of robot dancers, her popularity gradually began to wane. Deeply conflicted, she eventually came out against performances that included both human and robot ballerinas. No one took her position particularly seriously, since Ryzhova was known for being difficult, and the theater's staff had already grown accustomed to her flights of fancy. "You've cried wolf too many times!" Artistic Director Stefan Lastochkin once told his protégée.

Date: June 1, 1955 From: #daily_report To: Facility 3826 General Director D. Sechenov  New data from closed testing of AI project N. Even without the memories of the original, the subject shows unexpected reactions related to familiar items and events. Under certain circumstances, the AI displayed imitations of human feelings and emotions: anger, irritation, and even lust. This may raise questions regarding the ethics of copying human intelligence into an AI system, but it will most likely lead to reflection upon new dimensions of the study of empathy and ethics in AI.

Date: June 1, 1955 From: Assistant Manager of the Triton Complex Medical Block A. Ragin To: #observation_log  The experimental mechanic Dmitry Ploskolobov admitted with multiple injuries to the extremities and head trauma. An industrial accident. Ploskolobov decided to try out the experimental new SP4C3-LY type diving suit. Due to negligence, he fell while trying to get into the suit and was crushed by its structure. Preliminary diagnosis: blunt-force trauma to the head, stomach, and right arm; multiple rib fractures (TBC); simple fracture to the left tibia. Send for X-ray, then to in-patient facility.

Date: June 1, 1955 From: Museum Manager M. Yelizarova To: #reception  Good morning, colleague! Below is a list of the most important events for Dr. Sechenov to attend in the first week following the launch of Kollektiv 2.0.  List:  June 14: Moscow, Red Square. June 15 (evening): Great Pyramid of Giza. Global scientific conference (Nobel Committee, HoloLink only). June 16 (night): Joint lecture with Vavilov at Machu Picchu (in fact, it's a variety show, just for the record). June 17 (night): Speech on Easter Island, where robots will be building a statue of the scientist (speech from a hovering platform, then polymeric fireworks). June 19: Vovas parade along the Great Wall (no, it cannot be seen from space—that's nonsense). June 19: Chelomey fly-by of Mount Everest, live stream. Sechenov to land on Mount Everest.

Date: June 1, 1955 From: Museum Manager M. Yelizarova To: Argentum Data Verification Department  I'm writing to request the verification of available data due to the upcoming expansion of the VDNH exhibition zone devoted to flying cities. As you know, a number of major world powers came to us requesting the development and construction of flying platforms. Each of them, naturally, has its own characteristics and aesthetics. The Asian customers have requested the eco-friendly cities with parks, pagodas, and rock gardens, but no roadways. The USA, on the other hand, has requested flying factories-slash-"humant hills"—full-blown business centers like Wall Street. It's funny to imagine a skyscraper that literally scrapes the sky. We want to present all these projects to guests, but we need to know exactly which constructional details we cannot show, at least in order to avoid revealing trade secrets. Please have a look at the models and confirm what is permissible to be exposed to the public.

Date: June 1, 1955 From: Senior Lab Assistant F.S. Bloshin To: Facility Herald Newspaper Correspondent Comrade A.P. Golikov  "After receiving permission from the Party for the joint implementation of military space projects, significant steps were taken to put together programs for the exploration of near-earth orbit and space. The planning and calculations for launching third-degree robots into orbit—the Orbital Command Organizer (project name OCO)—are already in full swing. Robotics is not far behind, planning new robot models capable of working on the moon and even in antigravity conditions..."  Arkady, my dear, maybe something like this will do? I just can't keep rewriting the text twenty times over.

Date: May 1, 1955 From: Triton Complex Director J. Vernaya To: #secretariat  Decompression sickness has been eradicated. This illness, which has recently afflicted all employees after coming back to surface from Neptune, no longer poses a threat to anyone. Using polymeric modulation of air pressure, we were able to create a full-face mask that not only allows for rapid surfacing without consequences, but also working underwater up to 150 m without the use of nitrox or air-oxygen blenders. In relation to this, I have made the decision to equip the Neptune Research Center with new full-face masks. The Triton Complex will be first due to its exploration of the lake floor. And, of course, there will be training.

Date: June 10, 1955 From: Triton Complex Senior Sonar Operator E. Maximov To: Triton Complex Security Manager A. Kasperovich  I would like to direct your attention to the increasing level of interference in the bodies of water around the complex. I think the trilobites may be creating a polymeric suspension. I'm not able to verify this as all staff are busy eliminating the consequences of the breach. Please look into it; otherwise we'll be blind with no contact outside the complex!

Date: June 12, 1955 From: V. Yarkova To: S. Yarkov  We're alive, Uncle Sergey! Vitya, Alexey, and I are all safe and in one piece. I used the PEAR and saw you were online, which means you're also okay (I hope!) We don't know how things are over there at Chelomey, but we miraculously survived down below, underneath you. Vitya has been bitten by a Plyusch, but it's okay. We are waiting for the evacuation. Reply when you can. We're worried about you! Your niece and nephews.

Date: June 12, 1955 From: Procurement Department Manager R. Pleshko To: Sakhalin Testing Ground Security Manager I. Paramonov  Ilya, this is urgent! Besides us, a batch of M4D-5 neural puppets was delivered to the ninth hospital at Sakhalin. They're robot guards from Mendeleev. They were sent to help with repair work at Chelomey, but the operators messed up the logistics. My team is now shaking in their boots and refusing to work. What if another breach happens? The Mads are combat models, after all. We accepted and stationed them, of course. And now we're waiting for the papers to be corrected and the robots to be taken back. But I have an uneasy feeling. Be extra vigilant, okay? I might be overreacting, of course, but these Mads give me goosebumps.

Date: June 12, 1955 From: Monument Workshop Manager N. Davydov To: Chelomey Complex Secretary D. Tyomin  Comrade Secretary, regarding your request to design a monument to those perished during the robot breach... I believe this idea is extremely dangerous and wanton. Facility monuments are memorials to the triumphs of humanity's willpower and progress. We shall not immortalize tragedy, especially if it is caused by our own inventions. This would not be a memorial to the victims, but a monstrous confession of failure. We already have a wonderful tradition of glorifying the good and positive things and avoiding any opposition and criticism. So, let's be consistent and not make note of, and even more so, memorialize something distasteful to us and to the other people. Your request to design a monument has been denied.

Date: May 13, 1955 From: Technical Staff Officer V. Kislitsyn To: #complex_staff  Colleagues, I would like to remind you that the office refrigerator is not a storage area for expired meals! Your "toxic waste" causes tears even in the Vovas' eyes. A new rule will be in place starting today: on Friday evenings, everything that is left in the refrigerator will be thrown away by a janitor robot, regardless of the expiration date, and the forgetful owners will be [exterminated] admonished. Date: June 15, 1955 From: Triton Complex Security Manager A. Kasperovich To: Triton Complex Security Manager A. Kasperovich  To be honest, all the events of the last days are a blur. All these deaths, yelling, screaming as if through dense water... Every day, I thank fate, chance, or someone's will that we've managed to survive here at Triton. But to speak frankly, I'm grateful most of all that the MOR-4Y are autonomous and haven't turned against us... When one of the devices disappeared from the dock, I had already abandoned all hope. The soldiers were discussing which would be more difficult to handle: the Rafiks, Belyashes, or Dewdrops... Praise science that none of them—and us!—has had to see what the MORs are capable of if they were to go crazy like the rest of the machines. Damn it. I'm getting scared even as I write this. It's swimming around somewhere out there, after all. And who knows what could pop into that "orca brain"...

Date: June 15, 1955 From: AoC Radio of the Future Department Manager A.V. Lebedev To: Facility 3826 General Director D. Sechenov  I don't know if there's anyone on the other side of the screen, Dmitry, but I hope you'll receive my message. Fight fire with fire, as they say. As such, I am currently studying NORA's primary recombination protocols. I'm mulling over how to cluster reboot her system and, possibly, get the perfect weapon for this monstrous massacre... With a bit of luck, my creation will allow us to solve the problem created by yours. Although I don't believe in luck, I do believe in statistics. And despite all the consternation, it's on our side.
Date: May 17, 1955 From: Department of Ornithology Assistant Professor M. Illarionova To: Sakhalin Testing Ground Security Manager I. Paramonov

Date: May 17, 1955 From: Triton Complex Director J. Vernaya To: #for_publication  The multipurpose autonomous mechanism MOR-4Y is designed for underwater operation. It is practically the Burav's younger sibling but has a set of distinguishing characteristics. The majority of them are driven by the experimental conditions under which the mechanism must operate. In particular, the MOR-4Y is characterized by its highly durable body capable of withstanding an incredible amount of water pressure. Its astonishing mobility, provided by its independent, maneuverable modules, allows it to be used in such complex and precise work as laying underwater cables and pipes. Furthermore, if necessary, the MOR-4Y is fully capable of working on dry land, albeit with somewhat less efficiency. However, the main difference—and main achievement of Soviet scientific genius—lies in the construction of the MOR-4Y using a live orca brain. This is what makes such a complex system work.

Date: June 2, 1955 From: Assistant on Cultural and Educational Activities I. Kharlamov To: #facility_employees  Colleagues, this is a reminder that we will be holding a jubilee in September for the 10th anniversary of the Facility's Komsomol organization creation. The Komsomol cell from the Vavilov Complex will help us deal with all the arrangements—I am confident in this aspect. However, everyone else is expected to come up with suggestions for our organization's anthem. We've been around for 10 years, but don't have our own anthem, which I consider a failure. A Komsomol organization without an anthem is like children without names. I am putting particular faith in our Atomic Python stand-up club comedians. As a former comedian myself, I know you are creative, so you're the ones who have to answer first and foremost. I suggest you don't drag your feet. Summer is going by quickly.

Date: June 2, 1955 From: Triton Complex Director J. Vernaya To: Triton Complex Archives Curator D. Saydov  This morning, I read an article from a foreign newspaper about how Soviet science is changing the world and stumbled upon a curious fact: did you know that there is a Church of Kollektiv movement? Seriously, that's what it's called. It popped up three days after the launch. They support universal polymerization, hold virtual church services through the THOUGHT device, and do other things of that nature. On the one hand, it's commendable, since people are promoting the ideas of Kollektiv and such. On the other, a church?! Are you kidding me? You know, we're fighting against religion extolling mankind and its intellect and opening new horizons of science! And now someone's promoting that to the rank of "cult" and building a new religion around the ideas of progress and humanism. A couple of years ago, the USA also (loosely) combined religious and scientific ideas and got themselves the Church of Scientology. Quite an odious enterprise. To be honest, I don't think we need to follow that precedent.

Date: June 2, 1955 From: Senior Mechanic P. Plekhanov To: #techstaff_Triton  Hi, guys and gals (yes, ladies, I got it)! Updated instructions for the particularly forgetful (I'm talking about you, Grigorovich and Sevastyanova). There is an autonomous supply vessel floating on the lake. Are the lights broken or the cable gone? Use the control panel to send a signal. Need a new tool? Use the control panel to send a signal. Forgot your lunch on the shore? Well, you get it. The system will drop everything you need in a container. Other than organizational skills. You'll have to use your own!

First: the regular inspections of power sources like Candles at station number 13 were not put in place for no reason. Make sure they are always available there. Second: these freaking trilobites pick up everything that has even a speck of polymer, so keep the entrances to the observation stations closed. And third, if a trilobite still manages to get its pincers on a Candle, do not put yourself in harm's way. Call a specialist. Otherwise, we'll have to get the daredevil out of the trash again!

Date: April 23, 1955 From: Planning Engineer N. Zamuruev To: Triton Complex Director J. Vernaya  Dear Julia Albertovna, my colleagues and I have been discussing the construction of an underwater, swimming city similar to the flying cities. And we are so enthralled with this idea that we're ready to move from idle discussions to formalizing ideas and blueprints. Just imagine: Nereus, a giant underwater swimming complex for researchers and engineers. Like the Icarus Platform for Chelomey, but underwater. Extraction of oil and resources, exploring the sea floor, collecting biomaterials, and maybe even discovering new species! A project that aims to find new potential for humanity at the bottom of the sea will once again underscore the triumph of scientific thought.

Date: May 23, 1955 From: Head of the Inspectorate at the Ministry of Industry of the USSR A. Yakovlev To: Chelomey Complex Secretary D. Tyomin  Comrade Tyomin! We have discussed this already! I do not even accompany my children on the roller coaster or the Ferris wheel at the amusement park, and you yet continue to plot against me. How long must I tolerate this abuse? Every time you send the Turbine for me, I get soaked with sweat! There isn't even a parachute in your flying Wunderwaffe. I won't ask whose idea it was to fly ordinary cars in the sky, but I beg of you, my dear fellow: could you please arrange a less terrifying means of transport for me? Even a helicopter! As long as there is a parachute on board.

Date: March 25, 1955 From: Senior Lab Tech M. Isayeva To: Experimental Analysis of Behavior Group Director S. Mirina  Of all the individuals from group 58B, the most trainable is M236, Notus. He figured out the control panels within three days, completes tasks precisely, and ignores neural reagents as positive reinforcement, preferring to communicate. He stole one from me while I was having a quick lunch by the pool, and now he asks for them constantly.  P.S. Stepanida, I'm begging you not to put Notus through tests with punishment. I implore you not to hurt him. Please!

Date: May 25, 1955 From: Junior Lab Assistant V. Aleynikova To: #vetdepartment_Triton  Dear colleagues, please be advised: do not read the dolphins Russian classics, and do not allow them to watch scary movies! The mentality of dolphins is much more flexible and nuanced than ours. They easily pick up on negative emotions and become anxious and depressed. Please try to avoid philosophical subjects and deep discourse. It is best to only communicate with them simply, briefly, using jokes and funny remarks.

Date: May 25, 1955 From Triton Complex Director J. Vernaya To: Bioengineering Department Manager Dr. A. Morov  Dear Andrey Sergeyevich, I'm also not too pleased that your bioengineering achievement has been called trilobites. But that's how it goes, as you know. If it stuck, not even acid could erase it. Now, some criticism. Yes, the hybrids have successfully completed the tests and proven themselves capable of collecting garbage from the lake floor. They reliably find polymeric and neuropolymeric waste and deliver it for processing. But! They naturally drag in everything that contains polymer! They tried to carry off a polymerized employee, technician Korotkov, when he dove to the bottom while swimming in the lake. Please look into this.  P.S. In the official documentation, your project is registered as Limparius. It means "cleaner" in Latin, in case you weren't aware!

Date: May 27, 1955 From: Senior Oceanographer A. Polikarpova To: Triton Complex Director J. Vernaya  Put an end to the sarcasm and inappropriate irony! Yes, I am in all seriousness suggesting we use polymer whales as logical centers for the OCO project. So what? Picture this: enormous, majestic animals sailing through near-earth orbit. Their polymeric bodies harmonize with their unbelievably powerful brains, which we've improved with our neurotechnology. Isn't that impressive? You're saying, "Compared to the compact satellites and spacecraft, the idea to fill orbit with whales seems absurd and labor-consuming." When have we ever been afraid of work? Tell that to Comrade Stockhausen, who personally caught the first gray whale for Sechenov and laid the foundation for our work! The cosmic ocean, teeming with satellite whales, would be an incredibly powerful cultural phenomenon that's hard to imagine. It would be a sincere triumph of scientific genius and aesthetics. After all, it was the aesthetic part that made all the products and developments of Facility 3826 so recognizable!

Date: February 28, 1955 From: Salacia Complex Animation Studio, L. Atamanovsky To: Assistant Manager of the Triton Complex Medical Block A. Ragin  I can't take this anymore, Andrey. I'm tired. This Stockhausen guy is criticizing our work again! The director was even fired. Now we're wrapping up two new animated pieces with Artesha on orders from your complex. He says there's "not enough motivational propaganda for work and labor and too much artistic license." I suggested making something new, like an animated piece based on famous fairy tales, which he also vetoed. There's no life with his censorship. I'm going to ask for an exchange of experiences abroad, in the Land of the Rising Sun. I saw a few works from there—the animation is spectacular. And how are you doing at your challenging post?  P.S. Remember how I asked for a couple of tickets to the premiere of the new Lukomorye dolphin show? Were you able to get them?

Date: May 29, 1955 From: Trade Union Chairman E. Daukantas To: Manager of Testing Ground's Subsidiary Farming Y. Dynin #CC: Sakhalin Testing Ground Security Manager I. Paramonov  Yevgeny! There's a collective proposal to make our coastal area a leisure spot for Facility employees. You see, another bunch of vacationers from Mendeleev came back and are now in low spirits. They say there's real service there! They say there's recreation! We don't need much to start. A boat station with a pier, chaise longues, a couple of catamarans, and grills. Cover the shore with fine-grain sand or pebbles. It won't be cheap, of course (I've asked the accounting department to draft an appraisal), but the morale of the team is more valuable than temporary money. As the former manager of a Pioneers' camp, you know this better than I do. I'm planning to raise the issue on Monday at the staff meeting, so keep that in mind.  Hello and hugs to your Galina. Marina and I are expecting you for a barbecue on Saturday. Georgadze promised to treat us to marinated mutton!

Date: May 29, 1955 From: Senior Oceanographer A. Polikarpova To: Triton Complex Director J. Vernaya  Please be advised that ecologists have discovered a new mutation in a sea creature that has clearly arisen from neuropolymer supersaturation in water masses. This species (Octopus vulgaris, or octopus) can usually live out of the water for almost a day, but the subspecies discovered can go without for over a week. Additionally, this new "mutant" displays extremely aggressive behavior. In an attempt to obtain new neuropolymer compounds, it has been observed damaging cables, sneaking into the complex, and even stalking divers. Its self-preservation and breeding instincts are superseded by its hunger for neuropolymer. The females even use their own egg clutches to attack fish, dolphins, and divers with their offspring (we've named them octopups). I strongly insist that the issue of the swift extermination of the entire population be raised at the next meeting.

Date: June 3, 1955 From: Junior Lab Assistant V. Aleynikova To: Lab Tech R. Ivanova  Hi, Rimma! Yes, I know we just saw each other. I wanted to share an idea with you. Remember how we used to celebrate Neptune Day at Artek? It dawned on me today—why don't we bring that tradition here to Triton? Or even better, to the whole Neptune Complex! Imagine me and you as mermaids, the men in the costumes of sea devils, and Comrade Dynin in a sailor's shirt with a seaweed beard! I think it'd be symbolic and really fun. These celebrations really bring the team together. What do you think? Is it worth talking to Daukantas so he can bring the idea to the management? Or is it stupid?

Date: June 3, 1955 From: Land Oversight Services Manager D. Kirilenko To: Facility 3826 General Director D. Sechenov  Dear Dr. Sechenov, we have successfully concluded negotiations with representatives of the local administration of the Party secretariat. They have agreed to transfer a large portion of land adjacent to Facility 3826 for our purposes. However, we urgently need you to select the position for the new testing ground. Comrade Shalchinov, People's Deputy of Ozyorsk city, has requested a designated videodrome area on one of our testing grounds. He said you'd understand.

Date: June 3, 1955 From: Sakhalin Complex Senior Ranger P. Livadny To: Sakhalin Testing Ground Security Manager I. Paramonov  Dear Ilya Grigorievich, the pranksters are getting out of hand again. It's been two weeks since your lads caught the vandal who mutilated the beautiful Malus sieversii with the inappropriate and vulgar inscription "Yulia + Kolya." Well, we've got a new trouble! Someone excessively joyful has gotten into the habit of affixing eyes to the trees. Trust me, it looks quite creepy, especially at night! Not to mention that it causes damage to valuable and sometimes rare plants. Yesterday, a group of mycology students went out to the campsite at dusk and they were scared half to death. This is downright disgraceful, I'd say! Somewhere, the hills have eyes, as they say, so now our trees do? You must find out the identity of this prankster and let me know. I will prepare a report for their place of work or study. Then we'll see who's laughing.

Date: May 30, 1955 From: Triton Complex Head Veterinarian A. Sergeyeva To: Proposal Implementation Department Manager I. Kulibin  Dear Ivan Viktorovich, I have a quick question. Our dolphin Nale raves about soccer. He dreams of having legs. Sometimes, he gets so lost in his daydreams that he skips meals. As a result, he's become gloomy and is losing weight. I was thinking... Can your department invent some kind of... let's say, inverted dive suite with mechanical legs? Not to win any awards, other than the award of our daydreamer's good mood. Date: June 6, 1955 From: Chelomey Complex Assistant Secretary E. Nikishin To: Chelomey Complex Secretary D. Tyomin  Daniil, could you ever tell the difference in behavior between the Twins? Everyone says they're like two peas in a pod, reflections in a mirror, and other such "cut from the same cloth" expressions. But I've been working here for several years now, so I can spot the differences. Left is somewhat more... graceful, I guess. Her movements are smoother. More fluid. Date: December 8, 1954 From: Senior Oceanographer A. Polikarpova To: Planning Engineer N. Zamuruev  Comrade Zamuruev, our discussions have brought me to an interesting conclusion. And since I'm on sick leave now, this idea is occupying my mind nearly all the time. We already know that the depths of the World Ocean are explored much less than the far side of the Moon. According to various data, only 2–5% of the World Ocean has been explored to this day. I am in no way dismissing Wizard's aspiration for the stars, but if we want to study a cold, endless abyss, then we need to look down, not up. Furthermore, the likelihood of finding intelligent life at the bottom of the sea is, by all estimations, far higher than in space. What if we, with our wars, industrial revolution, and polymer, are just noisy upstairs neighbors? It might be worth getting to know all the residents of our house before going to visit. P.S. I've also sent my thoughts to the AoC. Maybe they'll look into this question. Please reply. I really value your opinion!

Date: June 9, 1955 From: Assistant Manager of the Triton Complex Medical Block A. Ragin To: #observation_log  The body of a scuba diver, Grigory Kainov, was brought in today. Right arm partially missing; it appears to have been eaten by fish or crabs. There was a lump in his stomach. When I opened it, some kind of octopuses jumped out (inexplicable). They began to run around the floor. I squished almost all of them. Scared the hell out of me. I need to urgently confirm with a specialist what these are and whether they have any kind of contagious capabilities. Preliminary diagnosis: too soon to tell. Contact Ganga complex's anatomic pathologist, W. Laurelova. She has also found something similar in a corpse this month (TBC). Note: I am incredibly tired. I want freedom. To sit on the deck drinking wine and discussing literature, and women in the evening.

Evolution's greatest strength is the so-called abiotic factor, i.e., the collection of direct or tangential influences from the non-organic environment on living organisms. I've been cooped up in our complex for six months already, and apparently, I'm going to die here. Could you say that we scientists, who are locked in this complex above which is the cascade of another complex—followed by the Facility—have become a new species formed by our own abiotic factor? My entire world is an endless series of labs, workshops, rooms, and hallways. I'm surrounded by a pile of scientific equipment, and I've made myself a spear from a floor lamp to fight off the crazy robots. Now I'm a new species fighting for survival with technology and my own workplace. What is this nonsense I'm writing? I'm going to try to get to the industrial sector. There were rumors going around that you can get out from there... if "out" even exists.

Addendum to lecture material, based on Moscow State University student questions:  ...Regarding the mannerisms of our production models, it's all much simpler and, as usual, a bit more absurd.  Rafiks and mittens The hands of the Rafik model were modified from cryogenic facility robots, in which the algorithm "cold = danger" reduced the risk of harm from supercooling. In the firmware of the model RAF-6, the algorithm concluded the opposite association: "safety = warmth." Later, in civilian modifications, the behavioral matrix was not eliminated. As such, mittens became something of a fashion signature for Rafiks.  Vovas and mustaches The mustaches were a side effect of earlier experiments on visual identification. The engineers decided to add mustaches because users trusted the Vovas that had them. The self-training algorithms solidified the component as an important social indicator among Vovas.  Tereshkovas and their "cute" tendencies Initially, Tereshkovas were given an "emotional mirror" behavioral template that included a positive reaction to round shapes, soft tones, and a conflict-free behavioral model. As a result of a too-flexible empathy matrix, this template developed into real attraction, which could be called love.  However, it is important to understand that none of this is "humanity," but an echo of old firmware left over from when we taught machines to imitate humans to make people more comfortable with them. Though I must admit, you will occasionally see a Vova trimming its mustache in front of a mirror. I wonder, have we inadvertently created something more than a simple machine?  Prof. Lebedev
